title: Tokens and Text Preparation · Level 3
slo: Prepare text for analysis by using tokenization and common preprocessing methods.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe lemmatization? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Lemmatization uses linguistic rules to reduce a word to its base form. Those rules help ensure the result is valid.
Lemmatization uses vocabulary as well as linguistic rules. This supports valid dictionary forms.
Simply chopping endings describes stemming. Lemmatization uses rules and vocabulary instead.

feedback.intrinsic: You could produce a form that is not a valid word.
feedback.instructional: Lemmatization aims for a valid dictionary form, not merely an ending-stripped form.

options.rationale: Labeling nouns and verbs is POS tagging. Lemmatization reduces words to valid base forms.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing POS tagging.

feedback.intrinsic: You would classify grammar instead of finding the required base form.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging assigns grammatical categories; lemmatization returns a lemma.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to produce valid dictionary base forms.

exercises.question_text: What is a corpus in NLP?

options.text: A body of text for analysis
options.rationale: A corpus is the body of language content being analyzed. It is the starting collection before it is broken into tokens.
Normalization can change punctuation or letter case before tokens are generated. It does not define the full body of content being analyzed.
options.better_fit: This fits when describing content after surface differences have been standardized.

feedback.intrinsic: You would mistake a preparation result for the full collection of content.
feedback.instructional: A corpus is the whole body of content; normalization is only one possible preparation step.

options.rationale: A sequence of terms treated as one group is an n-gram. A corpus can contain many such sequences.
options.better_fit: This fits when naming a phrase such as a two-word bigram or three-word trigram.

feedback.intrinsic: You would label one small phrase as though it were the entire collection.
feedback.instructional: An n-gram is a grouped sequence of terms, while a corpus is the body of content under analysis.

options.text: A grammatical label for a word
options.rationale: A grammatical label such as noun or verb comes from POS tagging. It describes an individual token, not the collection being analyzed.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying a token’s grammatical category.

feedback.intrinsic: You would focus on one token’s grammar instead of the collection to prepare.
feedback.instructional: POS tagging labels tokens; a corpus is the body of content containing those tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A corpus is the body of content selected for analysis.

exercises.question_text: Stop word removal changes every word to lowercase before analysis.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Choosing true would use the wrong preparation method for common-word removal.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Stop word removal excludes words such as “the,” “a,” and “it.” Changing case is text normalization.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Lowercasing is a normalization action.

exercises.question_text: Removing punctuation and changing words to lowercase can improve analysis based purely on word frequency.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: Keeping every surface difference can split counts that a frequency task may want combined.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Removing punctuation and lowercasing are normalization actions that can improve analysis based purely on word frequency.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Standardizing these differences can improve frequency-based analysis.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about n-grams are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: A unigram is a one-word phrase treated as a group. It is the one-term form of an n-gram.
A bigram is a sequence of two terms treated as a group. Multi-term groups can preserve phrase meaning.
A trigram has three words. A two-word sequence is a bigram.
options.better_fit: This fits if “trigram” is replaced with “bigram.”

feedback.intrinsic: You would assign the wrong group size to a phrase.
feedback.instructional: Remember the counts: unigram is one, bigram is two, and trigram is three.

options.rationale: Removing endings such as “ing” and “ed” is stemming. An n-gram groups a sequence of terms.

feedback.intrinsic: You would change word forms instead of preserving a meaningful sequence.
feedback.instructional: N-grams group terms; stemming strips endings to consolidate related forms.

exercises.explanation: Correct. N-grams are grouped sequences, and their names indicate the number of terms.

exercises.question_text: Reducing “running” to the valid dictionary form “run” is called ___.

parts.text: Reducing “running” to the valid dictionary form “run” is called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The chosen method would either strip endings without guaranteeing a valid word, standardize surface form, or add a grammar label.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Stemming need not return a valid word; normalization handles case or punctuation; POS tagging labels grammar. Lemmatization returns “run” as a valid lemma.

exercises.explanation: A valid dictionary base form is a lemma, and lemmatization uses linguistic rules and vocabulary to find it.

exercises.question_text: Put the pieces in the correct order.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The relationship between the process, its input, and its result becomes unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Place tokenization first, then the corpus it breaks, and finally the resulting tokens.

exercises.correct_answer: Tokenization breaks a corpus into tokens for analysis
exercises.explanation: The process must come first, followed by the body it acts on and the units it produces.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the parts to form the correct statement.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The timing of the preparation action is no longer clear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Name normalization, state its action, then show that it can happen before tokens are generated.

exercises.correct_answer: Text normalization can remove punctuation before tokens are generated
exercises.explanation: Normalization is a preparation choice that can occur before token generation, so the timing phrase follows the action.

exercises.question_text: What is “natural language processing” when treated as one group?

options.rationale: The phrase contains natural, language, and processing: three words. A three-word sequence is a trigram.

options.error_type: Miscounts the terms in the n-gram
options.rationale: A bigram contains two words. This phrase contains three words.
options.better_fit: This fits for a two-word phrase such as “artificial intelligence.”

feedback.intrinsic: You would group the phrase under the wrong n-gram size.
feedback.instructional: Count its terms: three words make a trigram.

options.error_type: Confuses a token with a term sequence
options.rationale: A token can be a word, partial word, or punctuation combination. This is specifically a three-term sequence treated as a group.
options.better_fit: This fits when naming one individual unit created by tokenization.

feedback.intrinsic: You would lose the fact that the phrase contains a sequence of three terms.
feedback.instructional: When three terms are treated together, the correct n-gram name is trigram.

options.rationale: Stop words are common words such as “the,” “a,” and “it.” This phrase can carry topic meaning as a trigram.
options.better_fit: This fits for a common low-meaning readability word.

feedback.intrinsic: You could discard a meaningful phrase while looking for topics.
feedback.instructional: Stop words are common individual words; this three-term phrase is a trigram.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Three grouped words form a trigram.

exercises.question_text: A social-media analyst sees important terms hidden among short customer posts. Which approach should the analyst choose to make key words stand out?

options.rationale: Words like “the” and “it” are common stop words. Excluding them can make key content words more visible.

options.error_type: Confuses stop word removal with normalization
options.rationale: Removing punctuation is normalization. It does not specifically remove common low-meaning words.
options.better_fit: This fits when punctuation details are not needed for frequency-based analysis.

feedback.intrinsic: Important terms may remain buried under frequent common words.
feedback.instructional: Use stop word removal when common words, rather than punctuation, are hiding key terms.

options.error_type: Confuses stop word removal with n-grams
options.rationale: Joining a phrase is n-gram extraction. It can preserve phrase meaning but does not remove stop words.
options.better_fit: This fits when the meaning of a multi-term phrase should remain grouped.

feedback.intrinsic: Common readability words would still compete with key terms.
feedback.instructional: N-grams group terms; stop word removal excludes words like “the” and “it.”

options.rationale: Frequency analysis counts how often terms appear. It does not exclude common readability words before comparison.
options.better_fit: This fits when identifying the most commonly used normalized terms.

feedback.intrinsic: The ranking may still give attention to common low-meaning words.
feedback.instructional: First exclude stop words when the aim is to make key content words stand out.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Excluding these common words can reveal the terms carrying the main topics.

exercises.question_text: A two-word phrase treated as a group is a ___.

parts.text: A two-word phrase treated as a group is a

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The phrase would be assigned to the wrong unit or wrong sequence size.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A unigram has one word, a bigram has two, and a trigram has three. A token is an individual unit, not the required two-word group.

exercises.explanation: The prefix “bi-” identifies a two-term sequence, while uni- means one and tri- means three.

exercises.question_text: A contract analyst must distinguish the person “Mr Banks” from common-noun “banks.” Which choices should the analyst make? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Lowercasing can remove the capitalization distinction between a name and a common noun. That distinction matters for this task.
Punctuation can carry meaning, including whether a word ends a sentence. It should be preserved when that meaning is needed.

options.error_type: Confuses meaning-preservation with stop word removal
options.rationale: Stop word removal focuses on common low-meaning words. It does not preserve capitalization or punctuation distinctions.
options.better_fit: This fits when important content words need to stand out.

feedback.intrinsic: The key name-versus-noun distinction could still be lost.
feedback.instructional: This task needs useful surface details preserved, not merely common words removed.

options.rationale: Stripping endings is stemming for grouping related forms. It does not protect capitalization and punctuation meaning.
options.better_fit: This fits when related word forms should be consolidated before counting.

feedback.intrinsic: You would alter word forms while leaving the needed distinction unresolved.
feedback.instructional: Stemming groups related forms; avoid normalization choices that erase meaningful case or punctuation here.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These choices retain distinctions that normalization could remove.
